name: Imperial Stone
lede: Imperial Stone is a dark olive brown named for a landscape word, stone, and is among the most common named colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A landscape word
sections.body:
The library records Imperial Stone from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, plate 14 K 7, first recorded about 1904 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[dusty-hazel]], [[antique]], [[orange-citrine]] and [[bistre-brown]], at 3.4, 3.5, 
In LCH terms it measures lightness 48, chroma 41, hue 85 degrees, the ISCC-NBS "light olive brown" block, Munsell 3.0Y 4.7/5.8, between [[brown]] and [[yellow]] [1]. 4, 3.5, 3.5 and 4.1 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 1,851 of 23,781 paintings, 7.78 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 1,071 [2]. That makes it more common than 91 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 52 of 945 paintings, at 5.5 percent of that century's paintings, 1.2 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often sits as an accent, in 49 percent of its appearances, by lightness rank [2].

Paulus Potter is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 10 of his 28 works here, 5.3 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [2]. The earliest match is dated 1125; that is 805 years before the name's own first record, in 1930, so the match is a look-alike hue, not evidence of the actual paint, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
